6. Bf1! is a surprising move that un-develops the Bishop, but by guarding the g2 pawn with the bishop the threat of ...Qxd5 is nullified.
Now if 6...Qxd5?!, White can calmly answer 7. Nc3 with tempo, and once Black's queen is driven from the a8-h1 diagonal, e.g. after 7...Qc5, White can then snap up the pawn after all, 8. Bxb5!, and Black has no threats.
Though 6...Qxd5 may be off the table, Black's knight is still en prise and this must be resolved.
Black may consider moving the knight instead. 6...Nd4 is the main move. The knight guards b5 and pressures important squares in White's position. White is best to shoo it away immediately, leading to a trade of knights: 7. c3 Nxd5 8. cxd4 Qxg5 9. Bxb5+ Kd8 ⩲. White wins back the pawn and has a small edge. This is a transposition into the Fritz variation, where ...Nd4 is played on turn 5.
Ulvestad's original analysis suggested 6...h6?!, a counterattack on White's knight that recognised that Black was better after either 7. Nf3? or 7. dxc6?. However, in 1963 it was discovered that White can play 7. Nxf7! anyway, the Kurkin gambit, and after 7...Kxf7 8. dxc6 has run away with the pawns.
Why not simply take the pawn back with the knight? 6...Nxd5, as played in Carlsen-Gukesh, 2024, is good and has become more popular in recent years.

r1bq3r/ppppk1pp/2n2n2/2bBp1N1/4P3/8/PPPP.text: Bd5 is often given an exclamation mark by theory books. This precise move gives rise to the possibility of  a future Bxc6 and overprotects the e4-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3P1n2/4p1N1/2Bn4/8/PPPP.text: White will still try to win the rook, but black can put a little fizz into it. 6. d6?! Qxd6 7.Nxf7? Qc6 8.Nxh8 Qxg2 9.Rf1 Qe4+ 10. Qe2 Nxe2(10. Be2?? Nf3#) 11.Bxe2 -+.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p2n2/2b5/4P3/2NP4/PPP2P.text:
6. Nc3? looks like a normal developing move. However, it is a mistake as it allows Black to play 6...Ng4!.
6...Ng4! threatens the pawn on f2. The only move to defend it is 7. Be3, though Black can take on e3 with their knight and then bishop, recovering the pawn. 7...Nxe3 8. fxe3 Bxe3⩱. Black is now even in material but holds a comfortable advantage because the bishop and threat of the queen swinging over prevents White from castling.
9. Qf3 is the continuation, but White must be mindful of other traps, e.g. 9. Qf3 Bd4 10. O-O-O? (thinking the king is best out of danger on the queen's side) Qg5+! 11. Kb1 Bg4 (pins queen to rook) 12. Qg3 (pins bishop to queen) Be5-+.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/2bBp1N1/3PP3/8/PPP.text:
Here Black can capture with Nxd5 and neutralize White's threat. Black is one pawn down but still has attacking chances, after 7. dxc5 Ndb4, for example.
Black can also try Nxd4!? here, allowing 7. Nxf7 because after 7...Qe7 8. Nxh8 sacrificing the rook, 8...Bg4! 9. Qd2 Nxd5 10. exd5 (trading the bishop for the knight) and 10...Bf5, the fork on c2 is inevitable and Black will win back the rook. However, if White plays 7. Bxf7 instead, Black will find themself down a pawn in an uncomfortable, albeit not losing, position.

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.text:
The bishop sacrifice is declined, not allowing Nxe4 with check. The position is now very unclear and both sides must play precisely to maintain their initiative. In addition, a fight for the center will likely play a big factor in the game for the next couple of moves.
Black should save their queen with its only move: 6...Qe7.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/n2Pp1N1/2B5/3P4/PPP.text: An attempt to fully hang onto the pawn. This variation does not inspire, giving up a good bishop for the currently out of play knight is not something many players would choose. Therefore this variation is seldom played.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n5/1B1pN3/4N3/8/PPPP1PP.text: 6...dxe4 captures 1 knight. All the other legal moves capture 0 knights.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
Time for Black to develop some more pieces. Spoiler: the pawn currently on d7 isn't going to make it to d5 at this point, because that would leave e5 hanging. So it'll have to go to d6 if the c8-bishop wants to get out.
The immediate 6...d6 would shut in the f8-bishop. That's okay, it's got a perfectly good square on e7.
6...Bc5 makes sure that the bishop doesn't get shut in, but becomes a pawn sacrifice after 7. Bxc6 bxc6 8. Nxe5.
If ...Bc5 is often a luxury Black can't afford in the Ruy Lopez, surely this applies double in the Schliemann Defence where the Black kingside has already been opened up with ...f5? Black's argument is that firstly, the open f-file is an attacking strength as well as a defensive weakness, and allows Black to fantasize about targeting f2 with ...O-O and ...Nxe4/...Ng4 to go with ...Bc5, so that gives White something to worry about. Secondly, the fact that the d-pawn is gone means that White doesn't have the simple plan of c3 and d4 with gain of time against the bishop.
If Black captures on e4 immediately, White has numerous strong options. 7.Nxe5, threatening 8. Qh5+, has to be met with 7...Nxe5, and then 8.Re1 wins the piece straight back with an ongoing attack (8...Nf6? 9.f4!) The immediate 7. Re1 or Qe2 are also strong, as 7... d5 allows 8.Nxe5. Regardless, the e file becomes a huge liability for Black with the king still stuck in the center.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2N2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPP1.text:
6...Qxf6 is a useful developing move - many writers caution against bringing the queen out early, but without the b1-knight on the board she doesn't have to worry about losing tempos to Nb1-c3-d5 or Nb1-c3-e4 ideas. Any opening that features a quick ...e5 and ...f5 (looking at you, Latvian Gambit) will likely involve putting the queen on f6 and castling kingside to bring a rook to f8 and then mating White on the f-file.

6...gxf6 has been played by FM Danko Bokan. You get the same pawn structure as in the 6.Qe2 d5 7.Nxf6+ line but White still has the option of putting her queen on a square other than e2.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4N3/5N2/PPP.text:
6...d5 is a beautiful freeing move in most 1.e4 e5 openings, and here Black gets it for free thanks to the awkward knight on e4.

6...Qe7 makes less sense, because if the queen is planning to capture on f6 then it's a waste of a tempo, and if the g-pawn is planning to capture on f6 then the queen isn't needed on e7 to defend the e-pawn because the new f-pawn will be defending it.

r2qkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1p5/4p3/4P1b1/5N1P/PPPP.text: This move looks natural, forcing Black's hand, but there is a surprising option for Black! 6...h5 is a surprising move that forces White's hand instead.

r1bqkbnr/1pp3pp/p1p2p2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2.text:
White opens up the center with this move and attacks the e5-pawn.
Black has two main moves, he can either take the d4-pawn with 6...exd4, or pin the knight with 6...Bg4.

r1bqkbnr/2pp1Bpp/p7/np2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
6. Bxf7+!
As we can see here, White played the unexpected move 6. Bxf7+!, sacrificing the Bishop to abuse the position of Black after 6...Kxf7 7. Nxe5 7...Kf6 8.Qh5 8...c6 9.Qf7+! & White has a huge advantage. This is known as the Nightingale Gambit. This is by far the most aggressive & sharp move after 5...Na5.

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n2n2/1p2p3/4P3/1B3N2/.text:
The move ...b5 is seen at some point in most variations of the main line Ruy Lopez, so Black has a few transpositional possibilities here: 6...d6 or 6...Be7 will probably end up in the standard Closed Variation (5...Be7 6. Re1 b5) and 6...Nxe4 almost certainly leads back to the Open Variation.
Basically, replacing ...Be7 with ...b5 means that Black has retained the option of setting up bishops at b7 and c5. The two independent moves, therefore, are the Arkhangelsk 6...Bb7 and the Møller 6...Bc5. They may transpose into each other.
It's always to Black's advantage to have something to play against the Lopez other than the old main lines, which is why these two sound, aggressive variations, along with 5...Bc5, have experienced a major revival of late.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n5/4p3/B2Pn3/5N2/PPP.text:
White is threatening to win back material by capturing Black's e-pawn. More importantly, they threaten to create dangerous attacks on the e-file while Black is still uncastled.
Black needs to complete their development, and if possible reinforce the crusading knight on e4. The immediate 6...d5? would leave the c6-knight pinned, allowing the powerful 7. Nxe5!. To get to grips with the situation, Black needs 6...b5 to prepare ...d5 by chasing the bishop away.
If Black is unconcerned with opening the e-file, they can accept an extra pawn with 6...exd4?!, the chaotic Riga variation, which leads to a wonderful mess.
6...Be7!? is a semi-useful move. After 7. Re1 this leads to a big liquidation of the centre: 7...b5 8. Rxe4 d5 9. Nxe5 Nxe5 10. Rxe5 bxa4⩲ and Black can't castle without dropping the e7 bishop.
Unlike in the Berlin defence, 6...Nd6? does not come with tempo on White's bishop and so does not work.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n5/4p3/B3n3/5N2/PPPP.text:
A minor sideline. Black's best move is 6...Nc5, and White can't preserve the bishop pair.
This leads to 7. Bxc6 dxc6 8. d4 Ne6 9. Nxe5 Be7 10. Be3 0-0 11. c4 and either 11...Bf6 or 11...Bd6, with an equal position.

r1bqk2r/1pppbppp/p1B2n2/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
By playing 4. Ba4 instead of 4. Bxc6, only to play 6. Bxc6, White has lost a tempo by moving their bishop twice. However, by waiting until Black has committed to ...Nf6, White prevents ...f6 to defend the e5 pawn (as in the Exchange variation, 4. Bxc6 dxc6 5. O-O f6). By also waiting until after ...Be7, White ensures that Black loses the tempo back if they defend the pawn with ...Bd6 (as in the Delayed exchange or Bayreuth variation, 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. Bxc6 dxc6 6. d3 Bd6).
After 6...dxc6 White can't win the e5 pawn straight because their e4 pawn is still hanging. First White defends their pawn with 7. d3 or 7. Re1. Black can defend e5 but give up their counterattack with ...Nd7, or pin White's knight to their queen with ...Bg4.
7. Qe2 also defends e4, but White still can't win the e5 pawn because of the tactic ...Qd4!.
7. Qe1 is an interesting alternative: this does defends against ...Nxe4 but White will still need to play ...d6 if they hope to win the e5 pawn due to the above-mentioned ...Qd4! tactic. Qe1 prevents Bg4 from pinning the knight. 7...Qg6 is probably best. 7...Bd6?! leads to 8. d4! exd4? 9. e5!. If 8...Qe7 9.dxe5! Bxe5 10. Nxe5 Qxe5 11. Qc3 Ng4 12. Qxe5+ Nxe5 13. f4! Ng6 14 .f5! (14. Be3 is also good) Ne5 15. Bf4 and White stands much better because of his better pawn structure.

r1bqk2r/1pppbppp/p1n2n2/4p3/B3P3/5N2/PPP.text: The plan is to hold e4 with the queen and move the rook to d1 in preparation for d2-d4, and again this has the drawback of putting the queen on the file most likely to be opened by Black.

Now the White's own e-pawn is defended, the threat Bxc6 & Nxe5 winning e5 becomes a serious problem for Black.
The main move, 6...b5, permanently cuts out any of that nonsense. Black usually follows with castling and playing ...d6, freeing their c6 knight from having to guard e5 and allowing their bishop to develop.
There's also 6...d6, the Averbakh variation. It looks like Black has just forgotten which order to play the moves in. In this line White can play 7. c3 before their bishop is kicked, so when ...b5 eventually comes the bishop can retreat to c2 in one move. White normally wants their bishop on c2, and this way they have saved a tempo compared to 6...b5 7. Bb3 followed by c3 and Bc2 later.
The advantage for Black is that after 7.c3 Black has time to play ...Bg4 before White has gotten in h3. Whenever a bishop appears on g4 in the Closed Ruy Lopez, White is going to have to play d3 and bring the queen's knight across to the kingside to drive the bishop away before considering d4. On the other other hand, Magnus Carlsen voluntarily plays d3 instead of d4 even without a bishop on g4, so the current verdict seems to be that 6...d6 loses a tempo for no reason.

r1b1kb1r/pp3ppp/1qn1p2n/2ppP3/3P4/P1P2N2.text:
Black develops the knight to h4 intending to manoeuvre it to the f5-square.
7. Bxh6? attempts to damage Black's pawn structure, but it fails because of 7...Qxb2 threatening to take the rook and only recapturing the bishop after 8. Nbd2. Black ends up being two pawns up in exchange for the slightly damaged kingside, which can be used to attack White with the newly opened g-file.
7. b4 is the proper response. After which 7...cxd4 8. cxd4 Nf5 places the knight on its target square.

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/1qn1p3/3pP3/3p4/2PB1N2/P.text: Black trades the pawn on c5 for white's d4 pawn. Black appears to be able to win the pawn but 7.cxd4 Nxd4? 8.Nxd4 Qxd4?? 9.Bb5+ would win the Black queen, so 7...Bd7! is the main move after 7.cxd4. 7.O-O is a modern gambit, sacrificing a pawn for quick development and an attack.

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/1qn1p3/3pP3/2pP4/P1P2N2/.text: Black stops White from expanding on the queenside with b2-b4 because of an en passant capture on b3. Furthermore, Black restricts White's f1 bishop range of movement.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/2ppP3/3P4/2PB4/P.text:
Black mounts an attack on the d4 pawn. Currently, they attack it with their c-pawn and their knight on c6, and they can bring another attacker with ...Qb6 should they choose.
White has two main options depending on how they configure their knights, depending on whether they wish to defend the pawn or not.
7. Ngf3, sometimes called the Korchnoi gambit or universal system, adds a defender to the pawn, but means that after 7...Qb6 White cannot bring another defender and the d-pawn is lost. It transpires that this gambit is sound: the continuation is 8. O-O cxd4 9. cxd4 Nxd4 10. Nxd4 Qxd4 11. Nf3 (defends e5 and allows White's queen to defend d3) Qb6, whereupon the choices are 12. Qa4, from where the queen may swing over to the kingside, 12. Qc2, or 12. a3.
7. Ne2 is the main line and traditional way to play. This develops the knight to defend d4 while keeping f3 open for the queen's knight, so if 7...Qb6 8. Nf3 cxd4 9. cxd4 there is no net loss of material.
Black's usual plan is to attack the end of the pawn chain with ...f6. The main continuation is 7...cxd4 8. cxd4 f6 9. exf6 Nxf6.
A final option to defend d4 is 7. Nef3. If 7...Qb6!? 8. Ne2 the line transposes to the 7. Ne2 Qb6!? 8. Nf3 move order. The difference comes after 7...cxd4 8. cxd4 f6 9. exf6 Nxf6, where White has the choice of 10. Ne2 to transpose to the main line or 10. Nh3!?.

rnb1k2r/pppnqppp/4p3/3pP3/3P4/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
This is an important branching point in the classical French defence. While the main line 7. f4 occurs in the vast majority of the games, the alternatives are not much worse.
7. f4, the aforementioned main line, has been called the Steinitz variation, though he usually preferred lines such as 4. e5, only playing the move once in his career. After being very rare in the 19th century, the move gradually became dominant over the others during the 20th century.
7. Qd2 is the Rubinstein variation, though it commonly transposes to the 7. f4 line. White seeks to quickly prepare queenside castling. Since queenside castling isn't safe for Black, it is not unlikely to result in a game with opposite side castling and vicious pawn storms on both sides of the board.
7. Nb5 is the Alapin variation. White threatens to fork Black's king and rook on c7. Black will generally at some point spend some tempi to chase the knight away. White will then have the option of rerouting the knight to a3 and subsequently c2, where it supports White's center.
7. Qg4, the Pollock variation, sees White quickly go for a kingside attack with their pieces. While objectively equal according to engine analysis, Black will have to be careful.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/4p3/b2pP3/1P1p4/P1N5/2P2.text:
By taking on d4, both White's knight and Black's bishop are now hanging. White has two popular responses in this position.
7. Nb5 threatens the d4-pawn and eyes c7. It can potentially move to d6, where it can't be pushed away by pawns. With the bishop still hanging, Black should retreat it. 7...Bb6 protects the d4-pawn, but not d6, where White will be able to put an uncontested knight. Therefore 7...Bc7 is more preferable, gaining a tempo on White's e5-pawn. After 8. f4, protecting the pawn, both sides should do fine with basic developing moves. White does generally exchange the knight for the dark-squared bishop when threatened (after 8...Bd7 9. Nxc7+ for example).

7. Qg4 is more aggressive. White leaves their knight hanging for now, and focuses on attacking Black's kingside, where the bishop is no longer defending. Black can't take the knight, since after 7...dxc3?? 8. Qxg7 Bc7 9. Qxh8 +- White is up a rook and Black's king is in danger. …

rnbqk2r/pp2nppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P4/P1P5/2P2PP.text:
Black places the knight on its best square.
Although Black's c5 pawn is not defended, White rarely chooses this continuation 7. dxc5, because then White's tripled pawns on the c-file are very weak and Black has an easy time regaining the pawn with 7...Nd7. White's usual continuation from this position is the aggressive 7. Qg4, which threatens to capture Black's undefended g7 pawn.
Alternatively White can also play the solid 7. Nf3 in order to prepare kingside castling, or they can play 7. a4 with the aim of developing their dark-squared bishop to a3.

rnb1k1nr/ppq2ppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P4/P1P5/2P2P.text:
Black develops the queen to the c-file, which may be opened up soon with cxd4. However, Blacks kingside still isn't developed, which can be exploited by White.
7. Qg4 is the main line and Whites most aggressive response. Here we see the second use of Black's previous move: Black can defend the g-pawn with 7...f6 or 7...f5, both of which open up the queens vision of the g-pawn. Alternatively, Black can play 7...Ne7, which transposes into the Poisoned pawn variation.
White can also go for a more positional approach with 7. Nf3, where it is more important to grasp the general ideas of the opening rather than hard lines. White can attack on the kingside with h2-h4-h5, while Black will try to trade the light-squared bishops with b6 followed by Ba6. White generally tries to get as much as possible out of this trade, usually using a combination of Bb5+ and a4 to take back with the a-pawn, placing it on the b5 square to restrict Blacks pieces.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/4p3/q1ppP3/3P4/P1P5/2P2P.text:
Black decides to poke at White's queenside, hoping for them to misplace their pieces. White's best option is to defend the pawn with 7. Bd2.
That is not the end of Black's plan however. After 7...Qa4 Black prevents White from pushing the a-pawn further and tries to keep White's queen stuck defending the c-pawn, though there are still some tricks.
8. Qg4 is the main line. White tries to get Black to weaken their kingside by either forfeiting castling rights with 8...Kf8 or by weakening the dark squares around the king with 8...g6. After either move, White can simply retreat the queen to d1, or play 9. Nf3 to castle kingside quickly. Losing the c2-pawn is usually not a big issue for White because they get a big development lead in return.
8. Qb1 is an alternative, looking for 9. Bb5+ to win the queen. Usually 8...c4 is played to prevent this plan and grab space on the queenside.
Apart from the slightly odd queen placement, Black can usually employ the usual ideas of the Winawer like ...b6 in order to trade off the light-squared bishops. White also has the common idea of h2-h4-h5 to start a king-side attack.

**History**
The variation is likely named after the players  Lajos Portisch and William Hook. Hook played this variation against Bobby Fischer who beat him and presumably gave some improvements.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3pP3/2B5/8/PB3PPP/R.text: Capturing the piece with 7. exf6 is both positionally desirable (threatening to ruin Black's kingside pawns) and tactically forced. Most other moves are punished by a combination of ...Bb4+ and ...Ne4, threatening a second piece. After 7. exd6? Qxd6 Black has the same number of pieces out as White (and two extra pawns), nor does White have any way in after 7. Bb5+? Nd7 (8.Qxd5?? c6).

rnb1kbnr/pppp1p1p/5q2/8/2B1Pp2/5Q2/PPPP2.text:
Black defends their f4 pawn and f7 pawn while developing the queen and blocking the f-file. This is the most testing reply to the Muzio Gambit as it forces White to prove sufficient compensation for the knight sacrifice. Black also carries the threat of 7...Qd4+ winning the bishop on c4. White must not let their attack fizzle out; for example, the most common move at club level is 7. c3, but this is too slow. There are other, better options available for White.

7. d3 is the soundest move for White in this position, but some players consider it slow. It allows the c1 bishop to view the f4 pawn, thus adding another attacker to it.
7. e5 often leads to chaotic play. More common that 7. d3 due to its aggressive style, this often leads to the Double Muzio Gambit, 7...Qxe5 8. Bxf7+, where White sacrifices their bishop as well.
7. Nc3?, the Bello Gambit, tries to distract the queen from defending the f4 pawn by tempting 7...Qd4+, but this simply does not work. After 8. Kh1 Qxc4, White can try either 9. Qxf4 or 9. Nd5 (the Baldwin Gambit), but they can be easily diffused: 9. Qxf4 Bd6-+ or 9. Nd5 d6-+ and Black is up two pieces.
7. b3!? is an extremely rare move which sets a somewhat dastardly trap; 7...Qxa1 8. Nc3 Bg7?? 9. Qxf4! and White is almost completely winning due to the undefendable f7 square and the queen on a1 stuck out of play, not able to do anything.

rnb1kb1r/pppp1p1p/7n/4N3/2B1Pppq/8/PPPP2.text:
Black chooses to defend f7 using their knight. This opening is called the Silberschmidt Defense. Despite the logicality and popularity of the move, this is not as accurate as the other main replies to 6. Kf1.
7. d4 is what most people play, taking the center and reinforcing the e5 knight. This is usually followed from the Black side by 7...d6 or 7...f3.
7. d3?? simply loses the knight to 7...d6!, trapping it as the d3 square is occupied by the pawn.
7. Nc3 is a minor try where after 7...d6 8. Nd3, Black has a slightly better position but White has more development.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1p1p/2n5/4N3/2B1Pppq/8/PPPP.text:
This accurate reply, named the Viennese Variation, deliberately gives up the f7 pawn to attempt to launch an attack on the White king on f1. White has multiple replies to this.
7. Nxf7 seems tempting — it wins the f7 pawn and traps the rook on h8. However, Black can start an attack on White's king with 7...b5! 8. Bb3 (8. Nxh8? bxc4-+ and Black is crushing white despite being down an exchange) Nh6! 9. Nxh8 Bc5! and White's king is struggling to survive.
7. Bxf7+ takes f7 with check but after 7...Kd8 8. d4 Nxe5 9. dxe5 Nh6 10. Bc4 Bc5 11. Qe1 g3! Black has a crushing attack on White's king that is survivable only with precision.
7. Nxc6 gives up the attack on f7 and instead trades knights, but it ruins the Salvio Gambit's idea of saving the knight and allowing Qh4+ to attack f7. After 7...dxc6, Black is better and simply fine.
7. d4 is the most accurate reply, taking the center and defending the knight. Black has a slightly better position after 7...Nxe5 8. dxe5 f3!, where 9. Bf4 is necessary because 9. gxf3?? leads a crushing attack on the White king with 9...Bc5-+.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5n2/3pN3/2B1PppP/8/PPPP.text:
White's c4-bishop and e4-pawn are forked by the Black pawn on d5. 7. exd5 is necessary to remove the threat.

7. Bxd5 would be a positional disaster for White. It would give Black a powerful centralised queen after 7...Nxd5 8.exd5 Qxd5, it would bring White no closer to recovering the pawn, and it would give up the bishop pair for no reason. In the analogous position after 7.exd5, 7...Nxd5 would not oblige White to capture the knight.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1bp1p/3p4/8/4PpNP/8/PPPP2P1/.text:
White's h-pawn is doomed. The only move that saves it is 7.h5, but there's a subtle problem with that move. Black has the secondary threat that after 7...Bh4+ 8.Nf2 Nh6, the next move is going to be ...Ng4 winning the pinned knight on f2 (or at least forcing the h1-rook to sacrifice itself for the bishop). If the White pawn were not on h5, White could offer some defence with 9.Qh5, chasing the pinning bishop away before the knight arrives on the scene.
Doing nothing at all would be a better move than 7.h5, but that's not allowed, so how could White make some use of this spare tempo?
You can postpone the decision one move with 7. Nf2, like Baron von Heydebrand und der Lasa did against Staunton, but there's no reason for Black to do anything other than grab the h4-pawn and transpose to one of the lines below.
7. d4 and 7. d3 threaten Bxf4, followed by g3 getting out of the pin. 7.d3 may be overly cautious compared to 7.d4, since there's no imminent threat to e4 whereas keeping the Black queen's knight out of e5 is very useful, especially if White's going to put a queen on f3 to help defend the kingside.
7. Bc4 is certainly in the spirit of the King's Gambit, making a bolt-hole on f1 for the king. But in this line, the king doesn't want to be on f1 particularly. …

rnb1k2r/pp1p1ppp/2p2n2/4q3/1b2P3/2NP4/PP.text:
This is very good for black as it pins the knight and threatens to exchange it to ruin white's pawn structure.
White now has:

7. Bd2 Unpin Variation
7. O-O Main Line
The Main Line (7. O-O) is better as it unpins the knight and moves the king to safety.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2p5/2b3B1/4n3/3P4/PPP2PP.text:
Black springs into action and offers their queen as sacrifice. Accepting it is poisonous for White, in fact Black has devastating continuations for all of White's moves.
If 7. Bxd8??, capturing the queen, Black has forced checkmate: 7...Bxf2+ 8. Ke2 Bg4#.
Unfortunately no other move for White is great either.

7. dxe4??, taking the knight, lets Black win White's queen. 7. dxe4?? opens the d file, and Black can force White's king away from protecting d1 to snap up their queen. 7...Bxf2+ 8. Ke2 Bg4+ 9. Kxf2 Qxd1 ∓.
7. Qe2 to pin the knight allows 7...Qxg5. White's best move is 8. f4: but Black can just trade down and go into an endgame up a minor piece. (8...Bf2+ 9. Kd1 Qg4 10. Nd2 Qxe2+ 11. Kxe2 Nxd2 12. Kxf2 Nxf1-+).
If 8. Qxe4+ Kd8 White must deal with both the threat of Re8, pinning White's queen to their king, and of Qc1+, infiltrating White's back rank (e.g. 9. Be2 Qc1+ 10. Bd1 Re8!).
If 8. dxe4?? Qc1+ 9. Qd1 Bxf2+ 10. Kxf2 (Ke2 11. Qe3#) Qxd1-+.
Therefore White's best seventh move is to prevent Bxf2+ by retreating their bishop: 7. Be3, giving up thoughts of winning Black's queen.
However, Black is winning even here, as after trading 7...Bxe3 8. fxe3 White's kingside is too weak. 8...Qh4+ 9. g3 Nxg3 10. hxg3 Qxh1∓ and Black is up a rook.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2Bnq3/8/PPPP1P1P/R.text:
White is completely lost. Black plays 6...Qxe4+, which allows for two options.
The worse of the two options doesn't seem the worst, but 7. Be2? allows the smothered mate (7...Nf3#) where the bishop is pinned.

Therefore White must give away the queen with 7. Qe2 and play on without that queen.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/1b6/nP2N1q1/2B1P3/8/P1.text: Black ignores the threat on f7 and instead counterattacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2. White can fork the queen and rook with 7. Nxf7, but runs into complications after 7...Qxg2!. 7. d4 saves the knight but doesn't save g2. Instead, the best move for White is 7. Bxf7+.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1b5n/nP2N3/2B1P3/8/P1PP.text: Black defends f7 with their knight and potentially preparing to castle. Most often in amateur play White plays 7. d4, threatening to remove the defender of f7 with Bxh6, however according to Stockfish, 7. Be2 is the best move.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2np4/b3p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/P.text: A solid move, defending the e5 pawn with their d7 pawn. White usually plays 7. O-O or 7. Qb3. 7. Bg5 is a sideline.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/b3p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/.text: Black counterattacks the e4 pawn with their knight, but this is not good. White should play 7. dxe5 to exploit Black's mistake and set a trap.

r1bqk1nr/p1pp1ppp/2n5/bp2p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/.text: An interesting gambit, Black sacrifices their b7 pawn to White's bishop on c4. The idea is that after 7. Bxb5, Black can play 7...Nxd4 where White's c3 pawn is pinned to the king, and unlike 6...Nxd4?, Nxe5 wouldn't be possible as the bishop on b5 is also attacked.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bn2n2/8/1PBpP3/2P2N2/P.text: Black retreats his bishop to b6. White cannot recapture the d4 pawn without hanging the b4 pawn. White can continue with 7. e5.

r1bqk2r/ppppbppp/2n2n2/8/1PBpP3/2P2N2/P4.text: Black retreats the bishop to e7. This retreat is generally considered safer, as it blocks any checks on the e file and controls the g5 square. Black will give back the d pawn and try to achieve d5.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/5N2/PP3P.text:
The bishop must move, and it did. This is actually the only not losing move. White has a couple options here.
7. Bd2 is a natural blocking move. Black can either trade and break the center with 8...d5, or immediately take with 7...Nxe4 which leads to complicated variations and the sacrifice of 8. Bxf7+!
7. Nc3 is a main line that sacrifices the e4 pawn. This is the Greco Gambit, where White then castles and gambits the pawn for development.
7. Nbd2 also exists. It was once very rare but has recently increased in popularity.
7. Kf1, also known as the Cracow Variation, is not usually played, as White can no longer castle and hangs the e4 pawn. For the pawn, White gains initiative and attacks Black who has to find only moves to keep advantage.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3p4/2Bpn3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
d5! simultaneously defends the e4-knight and attacks the c4-bishop. However, instead of retreating, White may try the move Bxd5! with hopes of Qxd5 Nc3! attacking the pinned knight on e4 and the queen, and cannot be captured as dxc3?? Qxd5! wins the queen.
A rarer followup is Nc3!! with the intention of dxc3 Bxd5! winning the knight on e4.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2B1n3/2p2N2/PPP2.text: This is the starting position of the Nakhmanson Gambit accepted. Black is now up 5 points of material and White must receive some kind of immediate compensation for their knight sacrifice. With their bishop directed right at White's weak f-pawn, they would love to play Qd5, an attack which threatens checkmate while attacking the undefended knight on e4. However, Black has the move 7...Nd6!, fixing both of these problems. Instead White must move their queen with check, leading to the move 7. Bxf7+! first needing to be played.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/5n2/1p1Pp1N1/2Bn4/2P5/P.text: Black kicks White's bishop. This position can also arise from the Ulvestad variation.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3np1N1/1bBP4/8/PPP2P.text:
6... Bb4+
Black tempts the pawn to c3 preventing the White Knight from developing.

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n3/8/PPPP1KP.text: Black plans to bring their queen out with Qh4 next move. To avoid any danger and move out of the open file, White has two sensible options: Kg1 and Ke3.

r1bq1r2/ppppk1pp/2n2n2/2bBp1N1/4P3/8/PPP.text: 6 .. Rf8. This rook developing move threatens to win the f2 pawn by Bxf2+, Kxf2 and Nxd5+ discovered check.

r1b1k2r/ppppqNpp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.text: White must now take their one and only opportunity to complete their fork and capture the rook before the game gains some complications. Otherwise Black will set up a very dangerous file with Rf8 aiming down at the king.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/5n2/nB1Pp1N1/8/8/PPPP1P.text: Blocks the check and threatens to exchange off White's aggressively developed bishop.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n5/1B2N3/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.text: White ties the minor piece count at 3 with 7. Nxc6. It's a free knight because if Black recaptures with the b-pawn, Bxc6+ followed by Qh5+ gives Black big problems.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.text:
Now that Black is no longer vulnerable to Nxe5 tricks, the e4-pawn needs to be defended. The economical-looking 7.Re1, normally a very sensible move in the Ruy Lopez, would be dangerous in the Schliemann because it would weaken f2, the target of Black's future pressure along the f-file.
7. Nc3 develops an undeveloped piece to its natural square. Nothing wrong with that!
7. Qd3 is a move that's recommended against 6...Bc5, because after 6...Bc5 7.Qd3 O-O?? White simply wins a piece with 8.Qc4+, so Black is prevented from castling for a while. However, there's currently no bishop on c5 to win, and if White wants to prevent Black from castling after 7.Nc3 she always has Bc4. White may also lose a tempo if Black's light-squared bishop comes to g4 and swaps itself for the f3-knight, because the queen could have recaptured directly from d1. On the positive side, putting the queen rather than the bishop on c4 has the advantage of maintaining the pin on the c6-knight that Black brought upon herself by playing 6...d6. Results-wise there isn't much to choose between the two moves.

r1b1kb1r/pppp2pp/2n2q2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPP1.text:
Having avoided committing the queen to e2 on move 6, White typically puts it there anyway with 7. Qe2. This restricts Black's options, because now ...d5 would self-pin the c6-knight allowing White to capture the e5-pawn for zero compensation.

Viktor Kupreichik mixed things up a couple times with 7. O-O. If Black reacts the same way she would after 7. Qe2, with 7...Be7, White has a huge positive score with the plan of Bxc6 and Qe1. But alert Black players found 7...Nd4! to take advantage of the fact that the e-pawn isn't under any pressure.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2n2/1B1pp3/4N3/5N2/PPP.text:
Aron Nimzowitsch would have been proud of the move 7. Nxf6, a "liquidation with gain of tempo", in other words Black doesn't have time to make a normal developing move if you capture her knight with check. Plus, she's going to have to recapture with the g-pawn to protect e5, and then you can point and laugh at the hole in her kingside pawn cover (and hope that her brilliantly supported centre is not as solid as it looks).
White has made a few attempts to avoid the exchange on f6:

7. Ng3 is possibly an underrated move. It makes more sense than the equivalent line 5...d5 6.Ng3, because the queen on e2 makes it impossible for Black to save her e-pawn. Having said that, Black was prepared to sacrifice that pawn anyway had White played 6.Nxf6 Qxf6 7.Qe2, so now she just sacrifices it differently.
7. Nc3 just invites Black's pawns further forward.
7. Neg5 has the idea that 7...e4 saving the pawn can be met by 8.Ne5 and White has two knights looking at f7. But again, Black doesn't necessarily want to save the pawn. 7...Bd6 8.Nxe5 O-O scores very well.
We should consider 7. Nxe5 too, because at first glance it looks like White is doing better than the equivalent 5...d5 6.Nxe5 line in having already gotten the move Qe2 in while Black has blocked her own queen from accessing g5. …

r2qkbnr/1pp2pp1/p1p5/4p2p/4P1b1/5N1P/PPP.text: After h5, black sacrifices the bishop for the betterment of Black's position. 7. hxg4? is bad because after 7. ...hxg4! the knight on f3 is attacked, and moving the knight is even worse. For example, after 8. Nxe5??, white captures the pawn, but  after 8. ...Qh4! the checkmate in four moves is unavoidable. White can also try 7. c3 with the idea of playing d4, but 7. ...Qd3 stops it. 8. hxg4, hxg4. 9. Nxe5, there is a move Bd6, attacking the knight. 10. Nxd3 and then, there is 10. ...Bh2+ and you repeat moves. And white can also play 7. d4 with the idea of developing queenside pieces.

r2qkb1r/1bpp1ppp/p1n2n2/1p2p3/4P3/1B3N2/.text:
Black elects to fianchetto his light-square bishop in order to gain pressure against White's kingside and center. This has the added benefit of defending the rook on a8, thereby taking some of the sting out of a future a4 thrust by White. However, the activity of Black's fianchettoed bishop can be countered by White overprotecting e4. Thus the most common reply by White in recent years has been 7. d3, after which Black typically develops his other bishop to either e7 or c5. The latter leads to positions which can also be reached from the Neo-Arkhangelsk (6...Bc5), though 6...Bb7 7. d3 Bc5 is the more common order. With a pawn on d3, White does not need to bring a rook to e1 in the near term, and so his queen's knight often travels to the kingside via c3 (from where d5 also becomes an option) and e2 rather than d2 and f1, since White does not wish to spend a tempo clearing the f1 square.
7. Re1 shares the idea of overprotecting e4 and allows White's queen's knight to take the traditional route; in this variation White intends to forge ahead with c3, d4, and Nbd2-f1-g3, though this knight maneuver will require the insertion of Be3 first if Black's dark-squared bishop has come to the a7-g1 diagonal. If White is not in a rush to develop the queen's knight, his dark-square bishop may instead develop to g5. This line is the oldest variation of the Arkhangelsk, having been played in the 1950 game in which Paul Keres, as black, sprung the then-novel Arkhangelsk on Alexander Kotov. …

r1bqk2r/2pp1ppp/p1n2n2/1pb1p3/4P3/1B3N2/.text: Black wagers that his dark-square bishop is more active here, while his light-square bishop may yet wish to develop along either diagonal. Transpositions to the Old Arkhangelsk (6...Bb7) are common, but there are independent lines involving ...Bg4 as well. White's main ideas in the position are a4, attacking the weak b5 pawn at once, c3 followed by d4, gaining central space and taking a tempo off Black's c5 bishop, or some combination. Also played, but less critical, are 7. Nc3 and 7. d3. The central fork trick 7. Nxe5 leaves white without the prospect of greater central control than his pawn on e4 can provide.

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p2p3/B2Pn3/5N2/PP.text:
Black ends White's pressure on the c6 knight.
7. Bb3 is necessary to save the bishop and the typical, automatic move.
From time to time some bright spark will wheel out 7. d5?!, the Richter variation, which can entrap Black if they avoid trading knight for bishop.
7. Nxe5!?, the Friess attack, can lead to a number of trades and an equal position. 7...Nxe5 8. dxe5 bxa4 9. Qd5 Rb8 10. Qxe4.

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n5/8/B2pn3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black takes on d4 and is temporarily two pawns up, but there is a loose knight sitting on an open file leading straight to their king. This leads to a wellspring of tactics and sharp play for both sides.
7. Re1 pins the knight and threatens to win it. Black must defend it with 7...d5 or 7...f5, and though White is winning the position is very precarious and many natural continuations are blunders.
The line to navigate through the pitfalls is 7...d5 8. Nxd4 (recovers a pawn) Bd6 9. Nxc6 (the natural 9. f3?? Qh4! is a massacre) Bxh2+ 10. Kh1□ (10. Kxh2?? Qh4+ 11. Kg1 and Black has a perpetual check between ...Qf2+ and ...Qh4+) Qh4□ 11. Rxe4+□ (an exchange sacrifice. The tempting 11. Nd4+ leads nowhere, and defending f2 with 11. Be3 is insufficient.) dxe4 12. Qd8+□ Qxd8 13. Nxd8+ Kxd8 14. Kxh2.
7. Nxd4?, recapturing immediately, lets Black off the hook, allowing them to trade the knights and simply be a pawn up. 7...Nxd4 8. Qxd4⩱ and Black's knight on e4 has time to get to safety.
7. c3, the Göring-style move, is just getting silly. This is a mistake as it allows Black's knight to escape while only recovering, at best, one pawn. 7...Nc5! 8. cxd4 Nxa4 9. Qxa4, Black gave back one pawn and ran off with the other and the bishop pair. Even if 7...dxc3? 8. Nxc3? (again Re1 was better) Nxc3!∓ White has traded off a pair of knights and is still two pawns down.

r1bqk2r/2ppbppp/p1n2n2/1p2p3/B3P3/5N2/PP.text:
Black ends White's pressure on their knight.
7. Bb3 is necessary to save the bishop.

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/1qn1p3/3pP3/3P4/3B1N2/PP.text: This is an obvious recapture and it also sets a devious trap! If black continues 7... Nxd4? 8. Nxd4 Qxd4??, 9. Bb5+ wins the queen.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/2ppP3/3P4/2PB4/P.text:
7. Ne2 defends the d-pawn while keeping the f3 square open for White's other knight. This means that 7...Qb6 8. Nf3 and Black doesn't have sufficient attackers to win the d-pawn.
White controls a lot of space. If Black plays a passive move, like 7...a5 or 7...Be7, White can play 8. f4 (there are other good moves), securing their space advantage.
The pawn chain is a nuisance for Black and they should like to find a way to break it down. Unable to win the d-pawn, Black must attack the end of the pawn chain with ...f6, and make progress towards improving their position that way. But first, Black must resolve the tension around d4.
7...f6?! immediately is inaccurate. Rather than answer 8. exf6, White has the option of 8. Nf4! (8. f4! is also good) threatening Nxe6 and Qh5+ to exploit Black's weakened kingside and king, who is still in the centre. Now 8...cxd4? is too late (9. Nxe6! Qb6 10. Qh5+ etc.). 8...Qe7 is the best try. (9. Nf3 fxe5 10. dxe5 Ndxe5 11. Nxe5 Nxe5 seems to win a pawn until 12. Qh5+! Nf7 13. Bxh7!! intending 14. Ng6 trapping the rook.)
7...cxd4 is a useful inclusion for several reasons. One is that it releases squares on the queenside where Black might like to put their knight or bishop, another is that it increases pressure on d4, because after 7...cxd4 8. cxd4 (8. Nxd4? drops the e-pawn), Black's pressure keeps White's knight tied down to defend d4.
After 8...f6, the main move, 9. Nf4? does not work because of this pressure. …

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/2ppP3/3P4/2PB1N2.text:
7. Ngf3 defends the d-pawn, but it prevents White from bringing their other knight to the defence of the pawn should Black increase the pressure. This gambit is sound for White.
After 7...Qb6, the most common move, White has no good way to keep the d-pawn defended.

8. Nb3?? c4! forks the bishop and knight.
8. dxc5? Bxc5 gives up space and helps Black to develop.
8. Qa4!? is an interesting try. If 8...cxd4 9. cxd4 Qb4! 10. Qxb4 Nxb4 11. Bb1⩱, White has held on to the pawn. Instead, Black can bring another attacker by chipping away at the end of the pawn chain, 8...Be7! 9. a3 f6 10. exf6 Bxf6⩱, and White must give the d-pawn up.
However, it transpires that sacrificing the pawn is sound, therefore the main move is 8. O-O and Black wins the pawn with 8...cxd4 9. cxd4 Nxd4 10. Nxd4 Qxd4. After 11. Nf3 (defending both d3, by discovery, and e5) Qb6, the main move is 12. Qa4.
12. Qa4 makes it hard for Black to develop cleanly, as the knight on d7 is pinned, and if Black develops their bishop, the queen can swing over to the kingside to pressure there: 12...Be7 13. Qg4! g6 14. Bh6⩲. Since Black is up a pawn they may instead wish to offer a queen trade: 12...Qb4 13. Qc2 Nc5 (attacking the bishop), then White can either engage in this little sequence 14. Bd2 Qa4 15. b3 Qd7 16. Be2⩲, or sacrifice the bishop in the hope of two pawns and a crushing attack, 12. Bxh7! g6 13. Bxg6 hxg6?? 14. Qxg6!+.
12. a3, allowing 12...Nc5 12. Bc2 but with the idea of b4, is an alternative. …

rnbqk2r/pp2nppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P2Q1/P1P5/2P2.text:
By playing 7. Qg4, White immediately attacks Black's unprotected g7 pawn.
Now it's Black's choice whether they want to defend the pawn, e.g. by playing 7...O-O or 7...Kf8, or whether they're
going to sacrifice the g7-Pawn and prepare some counterplay on the queenside instead. For this purpose
Black can try 7...Qc7, the Poisoned Pawn variation. This variation can also be transposed into via 7...cxd4.

rnbqk2r/pp2nppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P4/P1P2N2/2P2.text:
By developing the knight, White takes on a more positional approach. Because this move is less confrontational than 7. Qg4, Black has more options for dealing with it.
7...Bd7 threatens to put the bishop on a4, where it puts lasting pressure on White's c2-pawn. White usually prevents this with 8. a4. The drawback of placing the bishop on d7 is that the b-knight can no longer occupy that square, making dxc5 possible. This isn't too big of a deal, since it allows 8...Ba4 after which the knight can go to d7 and recapture the pawn.
7...b6 intends to trade off the light-squared bishops. White can prevent this trade with 8. Bb5+ Bd7 9. Bd3 but Black gets 9...Ba4 in. If White wants to prevent Ba4 they can play 8. a4 but this does allow Black to trade bishops with 8...Ba6. White can make things slightly more difficult for Black by not exchanging the bishops on Black's terms and playing 9. Bb5+ Bxb5 10. axb5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5P2/3p4/2B5/8/PB3PPP/RN.text:
Black will lose castling rights and have to play around a protected White pawn on g7 if she captures on c4 immediately.
So instead she throws in 7...Bb4+. In responding to the check, White must either give up the dark-squared bishop, block the  dark-squared bishop's diagonal, block the d-file, or forfeit castling rights herself. All of those are good things for Black!

r1bBk2r/ppp2ppp/2p5/2b5/4n3/3P4/PPP2PPP/.text:
The Stafford Gambit player's dream. White mistakenly accepts their queen sacrifice and now will be checkmated in 2 moves.
Black checks with Bxf2 and after the White king moves up, Bg4 is Black's win.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/3nq3/8/PPPPBP1P/RN.text:
The worst of the two legal moves, but White was losing anyway.

Black can immediately win the game with 7...Nf3#.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2np4/b3p1B1/2BPP3/2P2N2.text: An interesting sideline, White develops their c1 bishop and attacks Black's queen on d8. Black can choose from 7...Nge7, 7...Qd7, 7...f6 or 7...Nf6.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/2N2N2/PP.text: This is the traditional way to block the bishop check. With 7. Nc3, white does sacrifice the e4 pawn, but aims to get a dangerous initiative

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/5N2/PP3P.text:
This is a weird-looking move that seemingly doesn't make any sense. White can no longer castle and the e4 pawn is undefended. But the compensation exists. White has got a massive center while Black has none, and White are more prepared to attack than Black. The Cracow Variation a tricky opening, Black has to find the only moves to not to get a bad position. Black has several options:
7...Nxe4. Black has grabbed an actually free pawn. White can strike in the center with 8. d5!, kicking the knight back. After 8...Ne7 White has 9. Qd4, grabbing even more space, or a tricky 9. Bb3 with a threat of 10. Qd4 which is somewhy often unseen.
7...d5!. This is the strongest for Black option. After 8. exd5 Nxd5 9. Nc3 Black has to be careful to not to take the knight with their own knight. There is no reason to trade off a central knight. None. Instead, they should take the knight with the bishop, like in the Greco Gambit.
7...O-O?. After 8. d5! Black has giant problems with space and activity. In case of 8...Ne7 or 8...Nb8 White will go 9. e5!, completely paralysing Black, in case of 8. Na5 there is 9. Bd3 with an unstoppable 10. a3 and 11. b4.
7...d6??. This is a blunder. After 8. d5! Ne7 or 8...Na5 there is 9. Qa4+, winning the bishop on b4.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3B4/3pn3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
White plays the astounding Bxd5!! which seems to blunder a bishop. However, after Qxd5, Nc3! takes advantage of the two heavy piece pins and wins back the piece with a fork.
The only (natural) followup is 7...Qxd5.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1Bpp/2n5/8/4n3/2p2N2/PPP2PP.text:
Black  is in check and must capture the bishop with 7...Kxf7, which allows  White to play 8.Qd5 recovering the piece.
The attempt to evade the fork with  7…Ke7?? doesn't work; White plays 8. Qd5! anyway to defend the bishop, and the  threats of Re1 and Bg5 are crushing.

r1bq1b1r/ppp2kpp/2n5/3np3/2B5/5Q2/PPPP1P.text: White gives check and attacks the Knight. Black's king has several moves, but only one of them is good. The worst is         7...Kg8?? which loses to 8. Bxd5+ Qxd5 9. Qxd5+ Be6 10. Qxe6# (or 8. Qxd5+ Qxd5 9. Bxd5+ Be6 10. Bxe6#).  7...Ke8? doesn't work because of 8. Bxd5. Black has to defend the knight with Ke6.

r1bqk2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n3/4K3/PPPP2.text:
This is the move which modern chess engines prefer.
Black continues their plan with Qh4.

r1bq1r2/ppppk1pp/2B2n2/2b1p1N1/4P3/8/PPP.text:
7 . Bxc6.  The latest theory move.
The purpose of this move is to allow d3 to be played without the requirement to castle.

r1bq1r2/ppppk1pp/2n2n2/2bBp1N1/4P3/8/PPP.text: This is the natural move, defending the f2-pawn. White's king, however, has now committed to the kingside, which can bring some tactical possibilities to Black's play.

r1b1k2N/ppppq1pp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.text:
At the moment, White has a deceivingly uncoordinated attack on the Black king, but things can go very wrong very fast if Black allows moves like Bf7+ or Qh5+, preventing the Black king from ever castling to safety. For this reason, Black cannot afford a tempo moving their f2 bishop away or capturing with Nxe4. Instead, their best move is to cut off White's bishop with the move 7...d5.
This is not simply a free pawn, and leads to interesting offensive opportunities for Black.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2P2n2/nB2p1N1/8/8/PPPP1P.text: This inflicts isolated pawns on Black after the usual response 7...bxc6. 7...Nxc6 is playable but very rare as it does not gain a tempo on White's bishop.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B6/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black's queen is attacked, and capturing the attacker with 7...bxc6 will end in tears after 8.Bxc6+ Bd7 9.Qh5+! So we have to move the queen. Moving the queen to the fourth rank seems like a good idea, to try and neutralise the discovered check by hitting the b5-bishop, and at the same time cut out any of White's Qh5+ ideas.
Sure enough, the two variations from this position are both queen moves to the fourth rank:

7...Qg5 is the Classical Variation. The queen counter-attacks the helpless g2-pawn.
7...Qd5 is the Möhring Variation. The queen threatens the bishop and, indirectly, the knight with capture. White's only move to hold things together will be 8.c4, after which Black can argue that White's d-pawn is backward on an open file. Whether this is actually relevant with so many tactical possibilities on the board is another matter.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4P3/2N2N2/P.text:
Having put the pawn on d6, the only square available for the f8-bishop is e7, so it might as well go there immediately with 7...Be7. The c8-bishop still has options, and the option of breaking the pin on the c6-knight with Bd7 may be particularly useful, so it typically stays put for now.
7...Bg4 is also played, inviting White to transpose to 7.Qd3 lines with 8.Qd3 which gets out of the pin.

r1b1kb1r/pppp2pp/2n2q2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPPQ.text:
Attempting to defend the e-pawn with moves like 7...d6 or 7...Bd6 are ultimately futile. Either 7...d6 8.d4 or 7...Bd6 8.d4 (not allowing Black the trick 8.Bxc6 dxc6 9.d4 Bg4) just win it outright.

So instead Black gambits the pawn with 7...Be7. The compensation will be in the form of open lines for the rooks and an unopposed light-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2N2/1B1pp3/8/5N2/PPPPQ.text: It's check, and 7...gxf6 is necessary to regain the piece. 7...Qxf6 would be a bad way to sacrifice the e-pawn because White wouldn't be forced to give up the bishop pair in order to capture it (as she would after 6.Nxf6+ Qxf6 7.Qe2 Be7).

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p2p3/3Pn3/1B3N2/P.text:
White brings their bishop away from danger. It is well placed on the a2-g8 diagonal. Now White is threatening dxe5 to recapture the pawn. Rather than be greedy, Black should allow White to take the pawn back and focus on improving their own position instead.
White also has another threat. Three of Black's pieces are aligned on the same diagonal, and many amateur games have run afoul of ideas involving Bd5!, attacking both knights and pinning the knight on c6 to the rook on a8. If Black underestimates this danger they can lose quickly. Not uncommon in amateur databases are:

7...exd4?, thinking that trading is good when one is up material, makes the mistake of opening the e-file before Black has castled, and White is ready to exploit it. One line is 8. Re1 (pinning the knight) d5 9. Nc3!, threatening Bxd5, where 9...dxc3? 10. Bxd5! anyway.
7...d6??, thinking to defend the pawn on e5, allows 8. Bd5! immediately.
7...Na5? walks into either 8. Bd5! or  8. Bxf7+! Kxf7 9. Nxe5+ Kg8 10. Qf3.
7...Nxd4? is refuted by 8. Nxd4 exd4? 9. Bd5!.
As there is no good way to prevent dxe5 or hold onto the pawn (we've looked at 7...exd4? and 7...d6?; of course 7...f6? and 7...Qf6? are no good either), Black should give it back and make an improving move.
7...d5 is far and away the main move. …

r1bqkb1r/2pp1ppp/p1n5/1p1Pp3/B3n3/5N2/PP.text:
White leaves their bishop en prise to counterattack Black's knight instead.
Black can rescue the knight 7...Ne7 and it seems then White must play 8. Bb3 anyway. However, White has the devious move 8. Re1!, where the natural move 8...Nc5?, which preserves the knight and prepares to trade off the bishop, is an error: 9. Nxe5 bxa4?? 10. Qf3! threatens 11. Qxf7#. 10...f6? 11. Qh5+!.
In actual fact, allowing the trade of knight for bishop (either knight, 7...Ne7 8. Re1 bxa4 or 7...bxa4 8. dxc6) is fine for Black:
After 7...bxa4 8. dxc6 d6, forget about Black's potentially slightly rubbish rook pawns, one of which is an extra pawn anyway. Black has a stable centre, a half-open b-file, a kingside pawn majority that could quite easily wallop White after ...f5 and ...Nf6 and the bishop pair: it's one of those rare positions that are just really good fun (your mileage may vary).

r1bqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/p1n5/8/B2pn3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black is in danger of seeing some large pieces fall off the board in the next few moves. In addition to the piece currently en prise, the f3-knight is threatening to take on d4 ganging up on the c6-knight and freeing the f-pawn to advance to f3 and win the house.
Black has to start some sort of counterattack, and the way to do this is with 7...d5 ignoring the pin on the c6-knight. 7...f5 is too little too late (8. Nxd4 b5 9. Bb3 Qh4 10. g3 Qf6 11. Nxc6 dxc6 12. f3), and 7...Qe7 swaps one pin for another (8. Bxc6 dxc6 9. Nfd2 Bf5 10. Qf3 just about wraps things up). Anything else drops the knight.

r1bqk2r/2ppbppp/p1n2n2/1p2p3/4P3/1B3N2/P.text:
Black is no longer under any direct threat and may continue to develop. The king and c8-bishop still need to find better squares.
Of the three natural moves, 7...Bb7, the Trajković counterattack, is considered a sideline as it gives up the option of ...Bg4. White usually spends a tempo on h3 to prevent ...Bg4, and this move order lets White spend that tempo elsewhere. If Black's going to put this bishop on b7 early on, they normally want to have the other bishop on c5.
The main moves both carry threats of different types.
7...d6 is the main line. The d-pawn defends the e5-pawn a second time, freeing the c6-knight to come to a5 and swap off White's precious bishop. Therefore it "forces" the move 8. c3―a move White wants to play anyway―to give the bishop an escape square while preparing to advance the d-pawn. The main line continues 8...O-O 9. h3 and reaches a very theoretically rich position where Black has half a dozen serious continuations.
7...O-O first allows Black to follow up with the Marshall gambit 8. c3 d5!?. Black still has the option of 8...d6, and since in modern times 7...d6 is almost always followed by 8...O-O anyway, at first glance it seems that 7...O-O is a clear winner over 7...d6 in terms of giving Black options. That can't be entirely true, or no-one would play 7...d6. Firstly, the Marshall gambit has been analysed to death, and if there's a way of proving it absolutely sound it hasn't been discovered yet. …

r1b1kbnr/pp3ppp/1q2p3/3pP3/3n4/3B1N2/PP3.text: This seemingly obvious move is a mistake. Black just lost his knight to a discovered attack threat.

rnbq1k1r/pp2nppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P2Q1/P1P5/2P.text:
Black moves the king to defend the weakness on g7.
When this variation started rising in popularity in the eighties, players with White used to play 8. Nf3, after which Black can put more pressure on White's queenside with 8...Qa5 9. Bd2 Qa4 10. Ra2, after which Black has an easier time trading off the light-squared bishops, since White's usual response a4 for trading the bishops on White's terms is no longer available.
Nowadays, moves like 8. a4 and 8. Bd2 are more popular, which dissuade Black's plan of trading the bishops. 8. a4 does this by occupying the a4 square in advance, and 8. Bd2 does this by rendering 8...Qa5 ineffective, since it no longer comes with tempo on the c3-pawn, allowing 9. a4 ⩲.
Another popular response is 8. h4, preparing an attack on Black's kingside and allowing for the rook on h1 to be brought into the attack faster through Rh3.

**History**
The variation is named after Vereslav Eingorn who started using it in 1983, employing it many times in the following years.

rnb1k2r/ppq1nppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P2Q1/P1P5/2P.text:
Black lets White take the pawn on g7, but will break apart White's queenside in return. If White chooses to accept Black's pawn sacrifice, incredibly complex positions arise where general chess principles lose all meaning.
After 8. Qxg7, the main line, complications arise. The destruction of Black's kingside forces them to eventually castle long, where White has the open b-file to be used in an attack. Moreover, if all pieces are traded and an endgame arises, White will have good chances of promoting the passed h-pawn. Black will have to respond aggressively.
Less common is 8. Bd3, declining the pawn for now and preparing to castle short.

**History**
This variation was first played in 1945 between Vasily Panov and Viacheslav Ragozin. The game followed what is still considered to be the main line up to move 13, where Panov played 13. Be3. This can be attributed to the 7...cxd4 move order having been employed a decade prior already.

rnbq1rk1/pp2nppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P2Q1/P1P5/2P.text:
Although castling to the side where White wants to attack seems to be dangerous for Black, there are no
immediate mating threats - at least as long as White's queen is attacking Black's kingside on her own and without
support from other pieces.
That's why White usually decides to develop some additional pieces which may help with White's kingside attack. Typically this is done by playing 8. Nf3 or 8. Bd3, on rare occasions 8. h4 has also been tried. Note that 8. Bh6 is harmless for Black, who can defend against 9. Qxg7# by playing 8...Nf5 or 8...Ng6, in both cases White's dark-squared bishop must retreat and White wasted a tempo.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5P2/3p4/1bB5/8/PB3PPP/RN.text:
White has five legal moves to respond to the check. Ke2 is not the right one.
8. Kf1 is surprisingly popular, but the positive of  keeping lines open is outweighed by the negative of losing castling rights,  especially since the h1-rook can't get out via h3 while Black's unopposed light-squared bishop is watching it.
8. Nc3 looks natural, but 8...Qxf6! is a very cold shower. Far from stepping into a discovered attack, Black is setting up a devastating  cross-pin on the knight that White must waste several moves wriggling out of.
8. Nd2 means it's White, not Black, who will lose castling rights after 8...dxc4. Thanks to the threatened pawn fork on c3,  White won't have time to reinforce d2 with Ngf3.
So by a process of elimination we have 8. Bc3. This time there's a tactical flaw with 8...Qxf6, so Black must exchange bishops on c3 so as not to lose a piece.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1bBPn3/2N2N2/PP3P.text: Black accepts the gambit pawn, otherwise she will allow White to maintain a massive center. White follows her plan with 8. O-O

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3q4/3pn3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
Qxd5 recaptures the bishop. Now the only sensible response by White is Nc3, using the d1 to d5 pin and the e1 to e8 pin to fork the queen and double attack the knight.
As mentioned, the only move for White is 8. Nc3.

r1bq1b1r/pppp1kpp/2n5/8/4n3/2p2N2/PPP2PP.text: The  tactical point behind sacrificing the bishop on f7 is that White now has  8. Qd5+, regaining the piece (or one of the pieces, at  least).

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/8/1p1np1N1/3n4/2P5/PP1P.text: 7. ... Nxd5 Takes back a pawn and attacks the White Knight on g5.

r1bq1r2/ppp1k1pp/2p2n2/2b1p1N1/4P3/8/PPP.text: 7... dxc6. Taking with the queens pawn continues in Black's effort to maintain an active position, now the Black Queen is free to move on the d-file especially to the square d4 if required.

r1bq1r2/ppp1k1pp/2np1n2/2bBp1N1/4P3/8/PP.text: Allowing the Queenside Bishop to enter the game, the pawn moving forward now protects e5. The downside is that the exchange on c6 can no longer be taken with the d-pawn opening the d-file for the Black Queen.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n2q/4K3/PPPP.text: White must prevent Qf4+, leading to a swift checkmate. The only feasible option is 8. g3.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/2n2n2/3pp3/2B1P3/8/PPPP.text:
There are two main moves for White in this position.
The first is 8. exd5, gaining a pawn but allowing Black to create an attack on the kingside.
The second is 8. Kxf2, trading the bishops in hopes of moving the king to relative safety on g1.
It should be noted that 8. Bxd5 is a mistake because Bg4 traps White's queen!

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n2q/8/PPPP2P.text:
Checkmate with Qf2 is threatened. Surprisingly, the three strongest defenses, Qe2, g3, and h3 all give Black a perpetual draw (see below).

8. Qe2 Nd4 9. Qe3 Nxc2 10. Qe2 Nd4 11. Qe3 Nc2
8. g3 Nxg3 9. Nxh8 Nd4 10. hxg3 Qxg3+ 11. Kf1 Qf4+ 12. Kg2 Qg5+ 13. Kf1 Qf4+
8. h3 d5 9. Bxd5 Qf2+ 10. Kh2 Qg3+ 11. Kg1 Qf2+
This makes 8. Qf3 White's most popular move, although Black gains a strong initiative after Rf8 and with plans of rerouting their knight to g4.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p2n2/nB2p1N1/8/8/PPPP1PP.text:
This is the main line of the Two Knights Defence. Black has sacrificed a pawn but in return has gained a lead in development, as well as a better central situation.
White's bishop is attacked. It may be moved, or the attacking pawn may be pinned instead.

**Move the Bishop:**
8. Be2 is the old main line. White retreats the bishop to a square where it doesn't block any of white's pawns, but on the other hand, the white knight on g5 is vulnerable to being chased all around the board.
8. Bd3 is the modern main line. White blocks the d-pawn, but in return, gains the e4 square available for the knight to retreat, therefore this discourages 8...h6 because of 9. Ne4! in which White would gain an advantage.
8. Ba4? looks to be natural, but is in fact a blunder because of 8...h6 9. Nf3 e4!, in which white's knight either has to go back to g1, or move to e5, in which 10...Qd4 wins material.

**Pin the pawn:**
8. Qf3 pins the c6 pawn to the rook on a8, and also attacks the c6 pawn for the second time. Black can in fact play 8...cxb5 sacrificing the exchange for a massive lead in development, but more often continues with 8...Be7 or 8...Rb8.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.text: White turns the tables on Black with 8. Qe2, defending the b5-bishop and attacking the e4-pawn. The discovered check isn't as exciting as it looks thanks to the possibility of ...c6 in response. There's nothing to be gained by the panicked retreat 8.Nd4+ c6 9.Bf1, for example.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B1q4/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.text: Both of White's developed pieces are threatened with capture, so 8. c4 is necessary to distract the Black queen.

r1b1k2r/ppppb1pp/2n2q2/1B2p3/8/5N2/PPPPQ.text:
White accepts the gambit with 8. Bxc6, planning to capture on e5 once the guard is removed.

Castling kingside is still sub-optimal due to the ...Nd4 option (compare the position after 6...Qxf6).

r1bqkb1r/ppp4p/2n2p2/1B1pp3/8/5N2/PPPPQP.text:
8. d4, threatening the e5-pawn, is the move that really gets to grips with Black's pawn centre - given that 8.Nxe5 straight away is not possible because the White queen is pinned after 8...fxe5 9.Qxe5+ Qe7.
Krum Georgiev tried 8. Nd4, not to show off how many Black pieces White has managed to pin, but to threaten a queen check on h5 that would deprive Black of castling rights. It's not such a threat though, as ...Qd6 solidifies the c6-knight and makes room for the king on d8.

An improved version of 8.Nd4 is 8. O-O, which was played three times in the 2014 world rapid and blitz championships in Dubai. White postpones the decision about what to put on d4. If Black pre-empts Nd4 with ...Qd6, White can switch tack with 9.d4.

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p1n5/1p1pp3/3Pn3/1B3N2/P.text:
Black's position is now reasonable. If White allows them, Black is now ready to take twice on d4 and so cement their extra pawn of material. Therefore White must reclaim the lost pawn now, or have nothing to show for it.
8. dxe5 is by far the main way to do this. This exposes an attack on d5, which Black defends with 8...Be6.
8. Nxe5 is playable but uncommon. Black exchanges off the knight that is currently obstructing his c-pawn. 8...Nxe5 9. dxe5 c6.
8. Re1 would grant Black equality.
8. c4 is the extraordinarily rare Harksen gambit, where White sacrifices their c-pawn for either 8...dxc4 9. Bc2 where the knight on e4 is undefended or 8...bxc4 9. Ba4 where White's bishop is back on the a4-e8 diagonal.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/3p4/B2pn3/5N2/PPP2.text:
8. Nxd4 keeps the threats coming while recovering a pawn (White is two pawns down, remember).
8. Bg5 aims to eliminate the f8-bishop. It allows Black to break at least one of the pins against her king, but may still be good enough for an edge. ...f6 in response can get complicated.
8. c4 tries to pressure the center and eliminate one of black's d pawns. If black chooses to take en passant with ...dxc3, white can respond Nxc3, putting another attacker on the pinned e4 knight. The response 8...Bb4 9.cxd5 Bxe1 10.Qxe1 Qxd5 11.Bb3 Qf5 is more advisable for black.

r1bq1rk1/2ppbppp/p1n2n2/1p2p3/4P3/1B3N2/.text:
White's natural move in this position is

8.c3, continuing with the plan of eventually playing d4. This invites the Marshall Gambit ...d5 in response, which White may or may not be happy about.
Or White can try to do without the move c3, taking advantage of the fact that Black's c6-knight can't currently come to a5 and swap the bishop off because the e5-pawn would fall.
With the move

8. h3, White eyes a transposition back to the main line with 8...d6 9.c3, while reserving the option of reacting to ...d5 by quickly developing the b1-knight to c3, hence the name Ambidextrous Variation.
8. a4 is a radical change of course and was Gary Kasparov's choice. White takes advantage of the fact that Black a) hasn't forced the move c3, and b) can't play ...c6 because the knight is needed on c6 to defend e5, and hatches a plan of ganging up on the adventurous Black b-pawn with a4 and Nc3, while incidentally giving the bishop a retreat square on a2.

r1bqk2r/2p1bppp/p1np1n2/1p2p3/4P3/1B3N2/.text:
Whenever White opens with 1. e4, her most reliable plan is then to prepare to play d4. There is a very good reason not to play 8. d4? instantly - click and learn.
Instead, it must be prepared with 8. c3. With White's kingside fully developed there is no reason to delay this useful move any longer.
Note that h3 will be a useful move, but not yet - because it turns out that 8. c3 is also necessary to give the b3-bishop a retreat square. A White player who forgets her move order and plays 8. h3 is liable to have her bishop confiscated with 8...Na5.

rnb1k2r/ppq1nppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P2Q1/P1PB4/2.text:
White does not go for the craziness that arises from accepting the poisoned pawn but develops the kingside instead.
While White has a much easier time castling kingside, this may not be beneficial, especially when Black's kingside is opened up or far-advanced like in Carlsen - Rapport, 2024.
Black's main responses involve trying to force White's pieces onto "bad" squares.
8...c4 questions the bishop's placement immediately, forcing it back to e2 (9. Bf1 would be a waste of time). After this, Black has two options:
9...Qa5 puts more pressure on the queenside and forces White's dark-squared bishop to d2. This queen move is very thematic for the Winawer and is the central point of the Portisch Hook variation. Maneuvers for both sides can be observed in Shankland - Mishra, 2023.
Black can also go for the immediate 9...Nf5, waiting to see what White does and potentially transposing back to 9...Qa5 lines. In both lines, Black will be able to keep their kingside intact thanks to the knight jumping to f5 to defend the g-pawn.
8...cxd4 is more aggressive, often leading to more poisoned-pawn-esque positions. Black leaves White's bishop on d3 and allows White to eventually take on g7 because this pawn can no longer be defended with Nf5. 8...cxd4 requires White to respond with 9. Ne2. Theory continues 9...dxc3 10. Qxg7 Rg8 11. …

rnb1k2r/ppq1npQp/4p3/2ppP3/3P4/P1P5/2P2P.text:
White calls Black's bluff and takes the g7 pawn.
Black doesn't have anything better than 8...Rg8. The only alternative 8...Rf8? would be too passive.

rnbq1rk1/pp2nppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P2Q1/P1P2N2/.text:
With 8.Nf3 White develops an additional piece which can support White's efforts of attacking the Black King.
However, there is still no immediate threat for Black, so there's no reason for Black to play desperate measures like weakening their pawn structure on the kingside or something like that.
Hence they usually decide to develop more pieces by playing 8....Nbc6.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5P2/3p4/1bB5/2B5/P4PPP/R.text: Black is temporarily a piece down, and the bishop on b4 is threatened, so 8...Bxc3+ is necessary.

rnb1k2r/pp1p1ppp/2p2n2/4q3/4P3/2PP4/P1P1.text: Other moves lose material. Black can choose a variety of variations.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1bBPn3/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
White castles her king. This unpins her knight to her king, causing the black knight on e4 to be hanging. Due to the open e-file creating complications should black retreat her knight, black generally exchanges on c3. While …Nxc3 is appealing to keep the bishop pair, it enters the rabbit hole.
Therefore, Black should play …Bxc3, where after exchanging, there is no hanging piece, giving her time to play …d5

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3q4/3pn3/2N2N2/PPP2.text: Nc3! uses the queen to queen pin as well as the rook to king pin to fork the Black queen and knight, which will fall the next turn. Black most commonly moves the queen to a5 or h5.

r1bq1b1r/pppp1kpp/2n5/3Q4/4n3/2p2N2/PPP2.text:
White  has played the Nakhmanson Gambit, a hair-raising sacrifice of a whole knight  for an assault on the wandering Black king.
Good news for Black players: the Nakhmanson Gambit simply doesn't work.  There is a way to emerge from the complications into a peaceful position with  at least an extra pawn.
Bad news for Black players: the Nakhmanson Gambit is a nasty surprise if you haven't seen it before, thanks to this position.  The natural plan of retreating the king to e8, followed by  putting the bishop on e7 to shield the king from checks, is what White wants.  It allows White to escape with a draw even if Black finds the best defensive  moves.
Black's route to advantage instead begins with the ridiculous  8...Kf6! This just happens to work, though a player  searching for some principle behind it might note that the king is  temporarily immune from checks on f6, until the e4-knight is captured. This  means Black gets a crucial tempo to put a defensive piece on e7 without it immediately getting pinned along the e-file.

r1bq1b1r/ppp3pp/2n1k3/3np3/2B5/2N2Q2/PPP.text:
Attacking the central knight. Black must reply by moving the c6-knight to b4 (defending d5 with tempo and preparing c6).
8. ... Ne7?? is a huge mistake that lets white open the center with 9. d4! and strengthen the attack on the black king.
After 8. ... Nd4??, instead, 9. Bxd5+ followed by 10. Qd1 let white get back the piece and defend the c2 pawn. Black has survived the attack but is a pawn down with a very weak e pawn.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2ppp/8/1p1np3/3nN3/2P5/PP1P1.text:
8. Ne4. A testing move.
Now Black's Knight on d4 is at risk while the White Knight aids to the defence of the King side.

r1bq1r2/ppp1k1pp/2p2n2/2b1p1N1/4P3/3P4/P.text:
8. d3
While this is currently a theory move, it appears to be a mistake. White has difficulty to maintain an edge in this line. So perhaps appropriate is 8. d3?!

r1bq1r2/ppp1k1pp/2np1n2/2bBp1N1/4P3/2P5/.text: 8. c3. This move prepares d4 and allow the White Queen to develop along the d1-a4 diagonal.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/2n2n2/3Pp3/2B5/8/PPPP1b.text:
This is the best way for White to maintain a slight advantage. However, they must play the precise, correct moves in order to deter Black's many threats. This is because despite White's huge material advantage, they have barely any pieces developed while Black has space for both of their bishops, knights, and queen.
The first of Black's threats comes after 8...Nd4, giving the White queen no safe squares to move to.

r1b1k2r/pppp1Npp/2n5/4p3/2B1n2q/4K1P1/PP.text: The Black queen and knight are double attacked. However, Black has Nxg3, opening a discovery attack on the c4 bishop.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p2n2/n3p1N1/8/8/PPPPBPPP.text: White retreats the bishop to the natural square. It also partly protects the King side position.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p2n2/nB2p1N1/8/5Q2/PPPP1.text:
Develops the queen and pins the c6 pawn, as ...cxb5 gives Qxa8.
This variation has become popular in light of the game Nigel Short vs Mark Hebden in which Short won convincingly. However, computer analysis has suggested that Black has full compensation for the pawn.
Black now faces the prospect of giving up a second pawn or the a8 Rook in order to maintain a development advantage.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2pp1/5n1p/n2P4/2B1p3/3P1N2/P.text: Pins Black's pawn to Black's king, leaving it unable to capture White's vulnerable knight.

r1bqkb1r/p4ppp/2p2n2/n3p1N1/8/3B4/PPPP1P.text: Odd looking move, blocking in the d-pawn but the Bishop controls the e4 square for the Knight, therefore discouraging 8...h6. This has become the modern main line.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.text:
Black has to defend the e4-pawn, and does so with 8...Nf6, which has the additional benefit of covering h5.
8...Bf5 has a specific tactical problem: 9.f4! is a counter-sacrifice that White wants to play anyway, and with the bishop on f5 the pawn can't be taken: 9...Qxf4?? 10.Rf1 Qg5 11.Rxf5 Qxf5 12.Nd4+ is curtains. Plus, in the current position Black does have a secondary threat of ...a6 and ...Bd7 pinning and winning the c6-knight, which doesn't work if the bishop is away defending e4. Plus, f6 is almost certainly the best square for the knight anyway.
Another line that doesn't work is 8...Qxg2. The downside of playing ...f5 in the opening is the need to be vigilant about queen checks on h5. Here 9.Qh5+ g6 (or 9...Qg6 10.Ne5+) 10.Qe5+ punishes Black severely for her pawn-grabbing. 8...Nf6 cuts out this check, turning the illusory threat of ...Qxg2 into a real one.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B1q4/2P1p3/8/PP1P1P.text:
8...Qd6 is necessary to preserve the attack on the White knight. It's true that Black could have played 7...Qd6 in one move, but the move 8.c4 is hopefully going to prove to be a concession by White.

Horizontal queen moves like 8...Qg5 are inferior because the queen won't be hitting an undefended piece on b5 the way it would after 7...Qg5.

r1b1k2r/ppppb1pp/2B2q2/4p3/8/5N2/PPPPQPP.text:
Here's an example of how chess opening theory moves with the times.

8...dxc6 was by far the more common move until the mid-2000s. It seems logical to open a diagonal for the bishop that it can actually use, right? The same exchange in the Exchange Ruy Lopez is always met with dxc6.
But then along came Teimour Radjabov and revived the whole 5...Nf6 line based on the innovation 8...bxc6, and now every top player who tries this line - Zvjagintsev, Timmerman, Fressinet - goes 8...bxc6.
Why 8...bxc6 and not 8...dxc6? The intelligent answer is something to do with capturing towards the centre and pawn islands. The honest answer is that Black players tried 8...dxc6 and laid an egg, so they tried something different.

r1bqkb1r/ppp4p/2n2p2/1B1pp3/3P4/5N2/PPP1.text:
8...Bg7 is a deceptive move. Yes, it defends the vulnerable e-pawn - but not by attacking the square it's standing on, which wouldn't actually work because it would still have three attackers and two (non-pinned) defenders. Instead it defends the e-pawn indirectly by allowing ...O-O, which will unpin the c6-knight and, more importantly, allow the king's rook to come to the e-file and make the white king and queen uncomfortable.
8...e4 looks impressive but it just freezes Black's central pawns into a block of ice. White can play around the block of ice with Nh4, Bf4 and Qh5, or can play c4 which hits the block of ice with a hammer.

8...Bg4 is also not as powerful as it looks, because 9.dxe5 fxe5 10.Qxe5+ breaks the pin with check, and 9...Bxf3 10.Qxf3 just gives up the bishop pair for nothing. Possibly less than nothing, as it speeds up the White queen's journey to h5.

r1bqkb1r/2p2ppp/p1n5/1p1pP3/4n3/1B3N2/PP.text:
White recovers the pawn and exposes an attack on d5. Black must drop everything and defend the d-pawn.
8...Be6 is the best way. This defends the pawn, develops, and stabilises the centre.
For the sake of completeness, the other ways to defend the pawn are 8...Ne7 and 8...d4. Absolutely no Brownie points for either of these moves:
8...Ne7 is the Zukertort variation. This defends the pawn but doesn't develop a new piece and is slow. White can give up the bishop pair and still have a commanding position.
8...d4? is horrible. It pulls the rug out from under the e4-knight while not particularly improving the pawns condition. 9. Re1 Nc5 10. Ng5! with the idea of Qf3, and even winning the bishop pair is not enough to keep Black in the game.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/3p2B1/B2pn3/5N2/PP.text:
White's move threatens black's queen and attempts to eliminate the dark side bishop. Note that in the main line of the Riga Variation, that bishop is sacrificed on h2 for attacking chances on white's king.
8...Be7 accepts the trade, usually following 9.Bxe7 Kxe7 to break the pin coming from the a5 bishop.
8...f6 gets complicated. Now white has a piece in danger as well. White can respond Nxd4 and play can continue toward the main line. Simply moving the bishop again loses a tempo and the initiative.
8...Qd6 moves the queen out of the way, though it does take the square the bishop needs to sacrifice on h2.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/3p4/B2Nn3/8/PPP2PP.text:
Both Nxc6 and f3 are now threatened, and even if Black can meet the first threat there seems to be nothing she can do about the second, unless she can distract White by going after something more valuable than a knight. The departure of the f3-knight, an important defender of the White kingside, along with the strong placement of Black's own knight on e4, might be a clue...
The move is 8...Bd6, and the plan is for Black's bishop, knight and queen to have a chat with the White king.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1n5/3p4/B1Ppn3/5N2/PP3.text:
White has just advanced his c pawn into the center, threatening to pull one of Black's d pawns away.
Black can choose to take the pawn with either the d5 or d4 pawn, or ignore White's threat of cxd5, which intends to remove the defender from the pinned e4 knight.
If Black chooses to take en passant with 8...dxc3, White can respond Nxc3, putting another attacker on the pinned e4 knight.
The response 8...Bb4 9.cxd5 Bxe1 10.Qxe1 Qxd5 11.Bb3 Qf5 is more advisable for Black.

r1bqk2r/2p1bppp/p1np1n2/1p2p3/4P3/1BP2N2.text:
With White preparing to strike in the centre with d4, Black's king typically vacates the premises with 8...O-O. The old-fashioned move is 8...Na5, which may transpose, but the loss of control over d4 may allow White to save a tempo by omitting h3.
8...Bg4 is seen from time to time, discouraging an instant d4 by White. White will probably play d3 as a temporary measure, aiming to bring the queens knight to the kingside to evict the bishop in order to achieve d4.

r1bq1rk1/2ppbppp/p1n2n2/1p2p3/P3P3/1B3N2.text:
